questions.q: Why does the lesson argue against lumping 'total time for one VQE run' into a single number?
options: Because total time is impossible to measure
Because Python cannot time function calls

Because classical time (optimizer, Python overhead) and quantum time (circuit execution, queue wait) have completely different cost structures and different fixes, so a single number hides which one is the actual bottleneck
Because VQE loops never take measurable time
questions.explain: Classical and quantum portions of a hybrid program have fundamentally different costs and different remedies (code optimization vs. nothing you can fix in your own code for queue wait), so an undifferentiated total time number doesn't tell you where to focus effort.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say applying `cProfile` to a `backend.run()` call against real hardware is close to useless?
options: cProfile only works with simulators, never with any backend call
Because most of that time is queue wait and network latency, not time spent executing your own code, so cProfile faithfully reports 'waiting' without giving anything actionable
Real hardware calls execute too fast for cProfile to detect
cProfile cannot measure any function that returns a dictionary
questions.explain: cProfile profiles where your code spends time, but a real-hardware backend.run() call is dominated by queue wait that happens outside your process entirely -- cProfile has nothing useful to report because the delay isn't in your code's execution.

questions.q: In the worked example, why is it NOT contradictory that the same VQE algorithm profiles as 85% classical time on a simulator but only 2% classical time on real hardware?
options: Because the algorithm itself changes between simulator and hardware runs

Because the two runs measure genuinely different cost structures -- simulator runs are classical-overhead-dominated for development iteration speed, while hardware runs are queue-wait-dominated, correctly reflecting where effort should go in each context
Because percentages always sum differently depending on backend
It is actually a contradiction and indicates a bug
questions.explain: Both profiles are correct for their own context: optimizing classical code matters most for fast simulator-based iteration, while on real hardware the dominant cost is queue wait, which code optimization can't address -- the lever there is submitting fewer, larger jobs.

questions.q: What third profiling category does the lesson recommend tracking separately when a hybrid program targets real cloud hardware?
options: Disk I/O time
Memory usage only
Compilation time only
Queue wait time, separated from both classical time and actual device execution time
questions.explain: The lesson recommends explicitly separating queue_wait_time from device_execution_time (and from classical time), since conflating queue wait with either of the other two would make you chase a nonexistent code-performance problem.

questions.q: How does profiling (this lesson) complement resource estimation (Lesson 19), according to the lesson's closing section?
options: Resource estimation replaces the need for profiling entirely
Profiling is only used for classical programs, never quantum ones

Profiling tells you where time went after a run completes; resource estimation predicts resource needs (qubits, depth, shots) before submitting, helping reduce costly real-hardware submissions in advance
They are unrelated and cover entirely separate topics
questions.explain: Profiling is retrospective (where did time actually go), while resource estimation (Lesson 19) is prospective (what will this circuit likely need before you submit it) -- together they let you both diagnose past runs and plan to avoid costly queue-wait-heavy submissions.
